summary: FlameLens is an interactive dashboard that helps engineers and students find, compare and interpret NASA microgravity combustion investigations from the PSI database. Instead of browsing raw results, the user answers two questions: where will the crew live (lunar base or rover, spacecraft, spacesuit-like atmosphere) and what do they need to know (prevention, detection, suppression, or data for flammability models). FlameLens then ranks the investigations by fit, explains why each matters, and flags what is still missing, such as partial-gravity data.
details:
FlameLens: Which microgravity fire study should shape your habitat?

Fire is one of the deadliest risks in space exploration, and the Moon base atmosphere is expected to be richer in oxygen (30% or more, at 10.2 psi or less), which makes materials much more flammable. NASA has decades of combustion data, but it is hard to find, compare and interpret.

FlameLens turns that into a decision tool:

  • Choose a habitat context. Lunar base or pressurized rover, spacecraft or station, spacesuit-like atmosphere. An oxygen-versus-pressure chart shows how far each atmosphere is from Earth air.
  • Choose a need. Prevention (material flammability), detection (smoke and dust), suppression, or data for predictive modeling.
  • Get a ranked list. Each investigation (BASS and BASS-II, Saffire, SAME and SAME-R, DAFT, FLEX, CFI and CFI-G, ACME BRE and E-FIELD, SPICE and SLICE) gets a 0 to 100 score, its fuel and hardware, a short summary and a line on why it matters.
  • Read the interpretation. A plain-language recommendation names the three best starting points and states the known gap: PSI has no partial-gravity data yet.
  • Extract the data. The ranking can be copied as CSV for modeling work.

The score combines three ratings from 0 to 5: fit to the chosen need, relevance to oxygen-rich and reduced-pressure air, and directness to crew-habitat fire safety. The weights change with the habitat context.

Honest limits. The ratings are the team's qualitative assessment, read from the challenge description. They are not computed from numeric PSI measurements. Next step: load PSI test conditions directly so the ranking uses real values, and add partial-gravity results when LUCI and FM2 data are published.

Beyond space. Detection and suppression findings relate to terrestrial smoke detection, fire-water-mist extinguishers and firefighter gear, which NASA technology has already improved.
